Company hired for Trump’s reflecting pool makeover reportedly admits flaws in plan

Atlantic Industrial Coatings was given $14.7m no-bid contract and its findings contradict president’s claims of vandalism

Marina Dunbar
Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 BSTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 05.24 BST
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google

The company hired to renovate the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has acknowledged that “human oversight” and flaws in the repair plan caused the newly installed blue liner to peel and tear, according to documents reviewed by the New York Times that challenge Donald Trump’s repeated claims of vandalism.

The president has repeatedly said vandals armed with knives or box cutters were responsible for tearing apart the pool’s “American flag blue” liner. But documents reviewed by the Times show that Atlantic Industrial Coatings, the company awarded the renovation contract, blamed its own execution of the repair work and a flawed design plan.

The justice department has charged several people with vandalizing the pool in early July, but prosecutors began moving to dismiss those cases on 31 July. A federal court filing said information later supplied by the interior department showed the damage was caused by a flawed installation and the rush to finish the project ahead of the country’s 250th anniversary celebrations on 4 July, not vandalism.

The White House referred questions about the contractor’s report to the interior department. But in a statement, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said: “President Trump promised to make DC safe and beautiful, and he’s delivering.”

A spokesperson for the interior department did not directly address the report, but blamed “major vandalism” for the damage.

In a statement, the spokesperson said Atlantic was “contractually obligated” to remedy the repairs and was “well on its way to doing so”.

Atlantic Industrial Coatings did not immediately return a request for comment.

Atlantic first acknowledged its mistakes in a 14 August report and provided additional details in early September, according to the documents. As a result of “human oversight”, the company said crews failed to spray enough primer to properly bond the liner’s layers in certain places.

The company also said the design spelled out in the contract called for two chemicals to be used in separate layers of the liner even though the products ultimately proved incompatible. The chemical sprayed on top became hotter than the material below it could tolerate, causing the material underneath to blister and separate.

Atlantic said it had not anticipated that reaction because combining the two products in that manner was “very uncommon”.

Virginia-based Atlantic was awarded a $14.7m no-bid contract to repaint and waterproof the pool’s concrete floor in spring of this year. The approach had not previously been tested and was designed in part by the general manager of one of Trump’s golf clubs, according to the Times.

The renovation was carried out on an accelerated schedule as the administration pushed to have the Reflecting Pool completed before the nation’s 250th birthday on 4 July.

Atlantic has said it would repair the pool again under the project’s warranty.

Last month, Trump acknowledged the renovation had been rushed and that the contractor made mistakes, though he has not backed off his claims that vandals were responsible for much of the damage.

Writing on Truth Social, the president said the contractor had taken shortcuts while racing to complete the project for its 4 July opening. “As with many jobs, there was also some contractor error done by rushing the job,” he wrote, claiming that the damage caused by those mistakes was limited to “a very small area” and was “relatively inconsequential”.

‘Small price to pay’: the young homeowners welcoming falling house prices even as it hurts them

Some buyers say they are ready to absorb the fallout of housing weakness if it means boosting home ownership across the board

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Luca Ittimani
Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.00 BSTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 03.52 BST
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google

Falling property prices have come at the worst possible time for Alex Hogan and his partner. They are now weighing up whether they can afford to have another child.

Locked out of the established housing market, the Queensland couple resorted to buying a block of land to build a family home.

Fast-rising construction costs are now limiting their options and the anticipated value of their finished home is sliding, as rising interest rates and the government’s property tax reforms drag down property prices.

Yet Hogan wants the government to go even further in tackling the housing affordability crisis.

“If you don’t seize that momentum when there’s a push for it, then things can just go back to bubbling away under the surface and nothing ever gets done about them,” the 41-year-old says.

Although falling prices are frustrating many property owners, and price falls leave Labor vulnerable to political attacks, there are some homeowners willing to accept lower valuations in order to make housing more accessible for others.

Hogan is among several recent property buyers Guardian Australia spoke to who is prepared to absorb the fallout if it helps close the growing divide between forever renters and their landlords.

“It might end up sucking,” Hogan says. “But it’s better than having a two-tier society.”

Prices could fall 10%

House prices are falling across the country amid higher borrowing costs, a weak economy, and a once-in-a-generation change in the tax treatment of property investors.

The government’s critics have blamed the downturn on Labor’s May budget reforms, which included getting rid of negative gearing for new investors, excluding new builds.

“Australian families already struggling to pay their bills are now sitting at the kitchen table watching the value of their biggest asset, their family home, fall through the floor,” Tim Wilson, the Liberal Treasury spokesperson, said earlier this month.

Prices around Australia have fallen 3.6% from their peak earlier this year, according to Cotality data, led by steep declines in Sydney. The most expensive markets are falling the most, in a sign interest rates are a dominant cause.

Falls of more than 10% have been forecast by some analysts as elevated inflation makes a fourth rate hike more likely in coming months.

Most long-term homeowners have enjoyed years of growth, which has included a 26% price surge in just the three years to March. Newer buyers who missed the boom are most affected by the recent weakness.

Eibhlinn Cassidy bought a Melbourne apartment two years ago. They know loan repayments could spike when they refinance next year if the value of the apartment falls.

If you don’t have to sell at this point in time, that paper loss is just a theoretical one
Terry Rawnsley

Yet the 30-year-old junior doctor is stoic about the downturn if it makes housing more affordable because they remember the constant anxiety of grappling with soaring rents, weak tenant rights and losing bonds.

“I’d stress about it if it happened but, either way, I’ve got to be paying either rent or a mortgage and I’d rather be somewhere I can put paint on the walls,” Cassidy says.

“Even if I have to eat it, then big deal … I consider it a really small price to pay for a long overdue adjustment in the market that will let more people get in.”

Terry Rawnsley, a KPMG economist, says many recent buyers won’t have to refinance anytime soon and should be able to wait out the downturn. Prices are expected to rise again once the RBA starts cutting interest rates, likely in 2028.

“If you’re in a situation where you bought in the last 12 or 18 months, or you come into refinancing, you might be felling a bit of stress,” Rawnsley says.

“But if you don’t have to sell at this point in time, that paper loss is just a theoretical one and you don’t have to worry about it.”

‘I do not want to be a landlord’

Australian homes were turned into unaffordable wealth-building assets after a surge in prices in the 90s and early 2000s, thanks largely to favourable tax settings for investors.

Experts expect the current downturn and the loss of those settings to push the Australian mentality back in the other direction – in part because those who played by the old rules could soon find themselves in financial pain.

Remy Coll, a 37-year-old business owner, has become an accidental property investor after the price falls made it impossible for him to sell his old house.

When he bought in Canberra’s inner north earlier this year, he used his old home on the city’s outer fringe as collateral with a view to sell it soon after settling. The government announced its tax reforms the following week and, months later, the median Canberra home is now $44,000 cheaper.

Coll says he is now stuck with rising repayments on two mortgages, taking rent from tenants he doesn’t want.

“I do not want to be a landlord,” he says. “I do not want to contribute to the problem of rentals. But equally, now the house that I live in is contingent upon me getting a certain price for that house.”

Selling in the current market would mean he loses money on his first purchase, while potentially grappling with a higher interest rate on his second purchase as the bank revalues.

He and his partner are working extra hours and spending less time with their young children to hold on to their home as prices fall. He still believes the Albanese government did the right thing.

“That period of [price] reduction will be painful for probably a lot of people like me, and maybe some investors,” Coll says.

“But in the future, as long as real estate grows by a small amount [and] people’s wages grow more … people will be able to, in their early 30s, start to afford a house again.”

Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday. The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu. The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely. Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia. Scientists had warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica. 	html, body, div, span, applet, object, iframe,
	h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, p, blockquote, pre,

	del, dfn, em, img, ins, kbd, q, s, samp,
	small, strike, strong, sub, sup, tt, var,
	b, u, i, center,

	fieldset, form, label, legend,
	table, caption, tbody, tfoot, thead, tr, th, td,
	article, aside, canvas, details, embed,
	figure, figcaption, footer, header, hgroup,

	time, mark, audio, video {
		margin: 0;
		padding: 0;
		border: 0;
		font-size: 100%;
		font: inherit;
		vertical-align: baseline;
	}
	/* HTML5 display-role reset for older browsers */
	article, aside, details, figcaption, figure,
	footer, header, hgroup, main, menu, nav, section {
		display: block;
	}
	/* HTML5 hidden-attribute fix for newer browsers */
	*[hidden] {
		display: none;
	}
	body {
		line-height: 1;
	}
	menu, ol, ul {
		list-style: none;
	}
	blockquote, q {
		quotes: none;
	}
	blockquote:before, blockquote:after,
	q:before, q:after {
		content: '';
		content: none;

		border-collapse: collapse;
		border-spacing: 0;
	}

src="https://i.guim.co.uk/img/uploads/2025/07/17/Lisa_Cox.png?width=300&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=5c1fae211124e2c6370898220acd7ffe" alt="Lisa Cox" class="dcr-wso613"/></div><span class="dcr-scesqk">Lisa Cox</span></div></header><p class="dcr-1s160rg">South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. <br/><br/>
  The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday. <br/><br/>
  The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu. <br/><br/>
  The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely. <br/><br/>
  Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia.<br/><br/>
  Scientists had <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/aug/25/australia-has-just-12000-sea-lions-left-and-carnage-may-await-them-as-bird-flu-takes-hold-scientists-warn?CMP=Share_iOSApp_Other" data-link-name="in body link">warned of the potential “carnage”</a> in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica.<br/><br/>
  SA <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/aug/23/fur-seal-death-first-australian-mainland-mammal-h5-bird-flu" data-link-name="in body link">confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal </a>in August after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1.<br/><br/>
  John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, said at the time he feared the virus could quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">“The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">“I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population class="dcr-scesqk">Lisa Cox</span></div></header><p class="dcr-1s160rg">South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. <br/><br/>
  The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday. <br/><br/>
  The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu. <br/><br/>
  The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely. <br/><br/>
  Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia.<br/><br/>
  Scientists had <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/aug/25/australia-has-just-12000-sea-lions-left-and-carnage-may-await-them-as-bird-flu-takes-hold-scientists-warn?CMP=Share_iOSApp_Other" data-link-name="in body link">warned of the potential “carnage”</a> in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica.<br/><br/>
  SA <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/aug/23/fur-seal-death-first-australian-mainland-mammal-h5-bird-flu" data-link-name="in body link">confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal </a>in August after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1.<br/><br/>
  John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, said at the time he feared the virus could quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">“The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">“I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.”<br/></p><footer class="dcr-i9zbi8"><gu-island name="ShareButton" priority="feature" deferUntil="visible" developing MND at four times global average</strong></p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">People across a vast swathe of Australia are developing a deadly disease at more than four times the global average, AAP has reported.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">Researchers found a motor neurone disease (MND) incidence rate of 3.72 cases per 100,000 people annually across western NSW.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">In some areas, the prevalence of MND was up to seven times higher than expected, with several higher-incidence regions overlapping with areas of more intensive agricultural activity.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">The global burden of MND is increasing, and in 2021 the age-standardised prevalence and incidence were estimated at 0.77 cases per 100,000 people.</p><p class="dcr-1s160rg">MND was also observed to be occurring at higher rates in women than in other areas, and the incidence of bulbar-onset MND was unusually high.</p><footer class="dcr-i9zbi8"><gu-island name="ShareButton" Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy Cait Kelly (earlier) Sun 13 Sep 2026 06.02 BST First published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 23.59 BST Share From 14h ago 03.54 BST Confirmed case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion Lisa Cox South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday. The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu. The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely. Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia. Scientists had warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica. SA confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal in August after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1. John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, said at the time he feared the virus could quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions. “The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said. “I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.” Share Updated at 04.04 BST Key events 12h ago What we learned, Sunday 13 September 14h ago Confirmed case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion 16h ago Hanson faces bipartisan attack over resurfaced comments on Albanese’s mother 16h ago Albanese criticises Hanson’s ‘spiteful’ comments about his mother using public housing 16h ago Melissa Doyle appointed chair of Australia Day Council board 17h ago Joyce and Farley having ‘buyer's remorse’, Hastie suggests 17h ago Hanson ‘started a fight, and I intend to win it’, Hastie says 18h ago Anika Wells defends opt-out push for social media algorithms 18h ago WA police hunting for two men after shooting in Perth’s south-western suburbs 18h ago Bowen: Conflict in Middle East will impact fuel prices in Australia 18h ago Welcome 12h ago 05.50 BST What we learned, Sunday 13 September And with that, we are going to put the blog to bed. Before we go, let’s recap the big headlines. Energy minister Chris Bowen sought to reassure Australians about the nation’s supply reserves. He said Australia had 41 days worth of petrol in strategic reserve and 42 days worth of diesel. But he warned the escalating conflict in Iran would impact fuel prices. Speaking on Insiders, communications minister Anika Wells defended the opt-out push for social media algorithms, saying it was a “sensible measure to try and deal with these emerging harms that are coming”. Television presenter Melissa Doyle has been appointed chair of the Australia Day Council board. She said: “I am honoured. I’m humbled. I’m daunted. I’m excited”. Anthony Albanese said Pauline Hanson ’s comments that it was “not on” that his mother lived in public housing for decades. The PM said: “If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that’s fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson’s league, way out of it.” South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. Scientists have warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population, which is endangered, if bird flu takes hold. Thank you for spending some of your day with us. We will be back tomorrow to do it all again. Share Updated at 06.02 BST 13h ago 04.52 BST Sea lion dead from bird flu had been recovering from shark attack, minister says The South Australian environment minister, Emily Bourke , has given an update on the first confirmed detection of H5 bird flu in an Australian sea lion. Bourke said: We’ve seen quite a number of mammal cases, but the Australian sea lion is the rarest … found in our Australian waters. Eighty-five per cent of the population is found here in South Australia. It’s an endangered species, and today we are confirming our first case in this endangered species here in South Australia. She said the sea lion was recovering from a shark attack, but bird flu had caused its death. We found that it was actually not the shark attack that killed the sea lion. It was the bird flu case. We might find that this particular case was more susceptible because it was recovering. Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though one recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000. Share Updated at 05.24 BST 14h ago 04.16 BST Victoria launches ‘women’s pain standard’ for health practitioners A women’s pain standard to set clear expectations for how health services recognise, assess and respond to pain has been launched following an inquiry that uncovered systemic failings, AAP has reported. The Australian-first Victorian Women’s Pain Standard, announced on Sunday, will be embedded across the state’s public health services and aims to give women more consistent and higher-quality care. It follows an inquiry into women’s pain in November where medical gender bias and healthcare system barriers were laid bare, which was leading to denial or dismissal of pain, misdiagnoses or delayed diagnoses. The state government flagged it would develop a pain standard for women after the inquiry, which has now been created alongside clinicians, experts and women. Share Updated at 05.24 BST 14h ago 04.00 BST The South Australian government says there are three new detections of H5 bird flu, including the sea lion. The other new cases are a greater crested tern at Port Noarlunga South, and a little penguin at Victor Harbor. There have now been 290 confirmed cases of the virus in South Australia, from more than 2,000 tests administered by authorities. The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday. The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia. John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, said at the time he feared the virus could quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions. “The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said. “I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.” Share Updated at 04.04 BST 15h ago 03.18 BST Victorian Labor pledges to recruit 1,500 additional police officers The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll , has said the government will recruit an extra 1,500 frontline police if elected. The election pledge also includes building a new training academy in Melbourne’s south-west. He said: We know we’ve got to get more police on the street, community safety is my number one priority. This comprehensive plan deals with the how. This is the difference between the Liberal-One Nation policy on police recruits and Labor’s policy. Liberal-One Nation have promised more police. They’ve also said they’ll bring them from overseas. What Labor is promising is the pathway to unlock more police. With the second police academy to complement Glen Waverley.” View image in fullscreen The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Share Updated at 04.32 BST 15h ago 03.10 BST RBA expected to raise cash rate Comments by senior Reserve Bank of Australia officials will be closely monitored as anticipation builds towards another interest rate hike later this month, AAP has reported. The central bank’s chief economist, Sarah Hunter, will participate in a fireside chat at a Regional Australia Institute summit in Canberra on Monday. Then, RBA governor Michele Bullock will appear before a parliamentary committee on Friday. Both are expected to echo recent comments from bank officials reiterating that inflation is too high and leaving the door open to further interest rate hikes, after the three the bank has handed down so far in 2026. Hunter and RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser sent bonds markets into a spin in separate hawkish speaking appearances last week. Markets are now pricing in about a four in five chance the RBA will lift the cash rate by 25 basis points on 29 September. Share Updated at 04.31 BST 16h ago 02.33 BST Hanson faces bipartisan attack over resurfaced comments on Albanese’s mother Krishani Dhanji Pauline Hanson has come under fire from Liberal and Labor MPs for “appalling” comments attacking Anthony Albanese ’s mother that have resurfaced from an old podcast interview. The One Nation leader criticised Albanese’s mother, Maryanne Ellery , for staying in public housing for several decades, in a podcast with Karl Stefanovic from February this year. Andrew Hastie, who has had his own fight with Hanson, this morning criticised Hanson and told News24 she should “leave mums out of it”. I don’t think you should be talking about the late mother of anyone in this game, and certainly not reflecting on circumstances over which she had no understanding … I remember in the schoolyard, if anyone said anything about your mum, mate, it was on. So let’s leave mums out of it.” The trade minister, Don Farrell , also berated Hanson for the remarks this morning, telling News24: Anthony loves his mother, as I’m sure you do, I certainly loved my mother … To have them attacked publicly this way is just appalling. There’s a certain bitterness in One Nation’s approach to the world that I find quite un-Australian, actually. I think Ms Hanson should apologise.” Share Updated at 03.43 BST 16h ago 02.23 BST Albanese defends his mother as ‘way out of Pauline Hanson’s league’ The PM says he is “stunned at these comments”. But I’ll make this point. If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that’s fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson’s league, way out of it.” Share Updated at 02.28 BST 16h ago 02.21 BST Albanese criticises Hanson’s ‘spiteful’ comments about his mother using public housing The PM is back up where he is talking about comments Pauline Hanson made about his mother living in public housing. Hanson said in February it was “not on” that his mother had lived in public housing for decades, saying such housing “should be limited time”. This week she told the Australian, “The Prime Minister complains about his housing commission upbringing”. In response, he said: Firstly she made comments about me being complaining about being growing up in public housing. Nothing could be further from the truth. I’m proud to be a ‘houso’, and I’m proud of the community in which I grew up. I’m also proud about my mother. She was someone who had a tough life. She didn’t associate with billionaires. She was someone who as has been documented, when overseas, came back to a Australia chose to make the courageous decision in 1963 to keep a child out of wedlock. Who is now the prime minister of Australia. I said during the last campaign, kindness isn’t weakness. I’ll tell you what’s weakness – nastiness, and spitefulness. Share Updated at 02.36 BST 16h ago 02.13 BST Melissa Doyle is up now. She says: I am honoured. I’m humbled. I’m daunted. I’m excited. I’m every single emotion. But above all, as a journalist, as a storyteller, I have spent my entire career telling the stories of people who inspire us heroes. We all need to hear about extraordinary people doing extraordinary things in our community, advocating for us all in so many fields, be it science, be it sport, be it art, be it community leaders. I think we all need to hear those stories. And so to be able to play a role with the National Australia Day Council, to work with the board, to work with the executive, to continue to champion these extraordinary Australians and celebrate them and inspire all of us. Look, it’s truly an honour and I’m really excited.” Share 16h ago 02.10 BST Albanese: This is an important role for our nation. For decades, Australians have trusted Mel [Doyle] to tell Australian stories and now she will take that to the next level in the national interest. Australia Day is an important day where we come together. Share Updated at 02.14 BST 16h ago 02.08 BST Melissa Doyle appointed chair of Australia Day Council board Anthony Albanese is speaking in Sydney, where he has just announced that television presenter Melissa Doyle has been appointed chair of the Australia Day Council board. Share Updated at 02.13 BST 16h ago 01.50 BST People in western NSW developing MND at four times global average People across a vast swathe of Australia are developing a deadly disease at more than four times the global average, AAP has reported. Researchers found a motor neurone disease (MND) incidence rate of 3.72 cases per 100,000 people annually across western NSW. In some areas, the prevalence of MND was up to seven times higher than expected, with several higher-incidence regions overlapping with areas of more intensive agricultural activity. The global burden of MND is increasing, and in 2021 the age-standardised prevalence and incidence were estimated at 0.77 cases per 100,000 people. MND was also observed to be occurring at higher rates in women than in other areas, and the incidence of bulbar-onset MND was unusually high. Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday. The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu. The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely. Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia. Scientists had warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica. liveBlogUpdate.headline: First case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion confirmed – as it happened
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Sea lion dead from bird flu had been recovering from shark attack, minister says The South Australian environment minister, Emily Bourke, has given an update on the first confirmed detection of H5 bird flu in an Australian sea lion. Bourke said: We’ve seen quite a number of mammal cases, but the Australian sea lion is the rarest … found in our Australian waters. Eighty-five per cent of the population is found here in South Australia. It’s an endangered species, and today we are confirming our first case in this endangered species here in South Australia. She said the sea lion was recovering from a shark attack, but bird flu had caused its death. We found that it was actually not the shark attack that killed the sea lion. It was the bird flu case. We might find that this particular case was more susceptible because it was recovering. Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though one recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000.

liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Victoria launches ‘women’s pain standard’ for health practitioners A women’s pain standard to set clear expectations for how health services recognise, assess and respond to pain has been launched following an inquiry that uncovered systemic failings, AAP has reported. The Australian-first Victorian Women’s Pain Standard, announced on Sunday, will be embedded across the state’s public health services and aims to give women more consistent and higher-quality care. It follows an inquiry into women’s pain in November where medical gender bias and healthcare system barriers were laid bare, which was leading to denial or dismissal of pain, misdiagnoses or delayed diagnoses. The state government flagged it would develop a pain standard for women after the inquiry, which has now been created alongside clinicians, experts and women.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: First case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion confirmed – as it happened
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: The South Australian government says there are three new detections of H5 bird flu, including the sea lion. The other new cases are a greater crested tern at Port Noarlunga South, and a little penguin at Victor Harbor. There have now been 290 confirmed cases of the virus in South Australia, from more than 2,000 tests administered by authorities.

liveBlogUpdate.headline: First case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion confirmed – as it happened
liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday. The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu. The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely. Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia. Scientists had warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica. liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: Victorian Labor pledges to recruit 1,500 additional police officers The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has said the government will recruit an extra 1,500 frontline police if elected. The election pledge also includes building a new training academy in Melbourne’s south-west. He said: We know we’ve got to get more police on the street, community safety is my number one priority. This comprehensive plan deals with the how. This is the difference between the Liberal-One Nation policy on police recruits and Labor’s policy. Liberal-One Nation have promised more police. They’ve also said they’ll bring them from overseas. What Labor is promising is the pathway to unlock more police. With the second police academy to complement Glen Waverley.”

liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: RBA expected to raise cash rate Comments by senior Reserve Bank of Australia officials will be closely monitored as anticipation builds towards another interest rate hike later this month, AAP has reported. The central bank’s chief economist, Sarah Hunter, will participate in a fireside chat at a Regional Australia Institute summit in Canberra on Monday. Then, RBA governor Michele Bullock will appear before a parliamentary committee on Friday. Both are expected to echo recent comments from bank officials reiterating that inflation is too high and leaving the door open to further interest rate hikes, after the three the bank has handed down so far in 2026. Hunter and RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser sent bonds markets into a spin in separate hawkish speaking appearances last week. Markets are now pricing in about a four in five chance the RBA will lift the cash rate by 25 basis points on 29 September.

liveBlogUpdate.articleBody: People in western NSW developing MND at four times global average People across a vast swathe of Australia are developing a deadly disease at more than four times the global average, AAP has reported. Researchers found a motor neurone disease (MND) incidence rate of 3.72 cases per 100,000 people annually across western NSW. In some areas, the prevalence of MND was up to seven times higher than expected, with several higher-incidence regions overlapping with areas of more intensive agricultural activity. The global burden of MND is increasing, and in 2021 the age-standardised prevalence and incidence were estimated at 0.77 cases per 100,000 people. MND was also observed to be occurring at higher rates in women than in other areas, and the incidence of bulbar-onset MND was unusually high.

Explainer

How to use the Guardian University Guide 2027

Don’t be overwhelmed by the choice on offer – use this guide to help make a selection

  • The 2027 league table

  • View the full guide

Rachel Hall
Sat 12 Sep 2026 07.58 BST
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google

Welcome to the Guardian University Guide 2027. It’s a big, expensive decision to go to university – and in the middle of a graduate jobs crisis, the stakes have never felt higher.

This year’s guide will help you figure out how to make going to university worth it, from which courses offer the best AI-proof job prospects, to how you can cut costs by living at home.

The Guardian rankings will help you figure out which universities give their students the best experience, rather than just showing you which are strongest in academic research, like most other league tables.

We rank universities through eight different scores, which form a total out of 100. These include what students say about their teaching and feedback in the annual National Student Survey.

We also look at how big class sizes are through the student-to-staff ratio and how much universities spend on teaching each student. Other areas covered are students’ A-level grades and whether their academic performance improves at university (the value-added score), and how likely they are to persevere with their course. There’s also data on how many students get graduate jobs 15 months after leaving university. For each metric, we use the most recent data available at the time of publication. Any blank spaces mean there is data missing, so we focus on the other measures.

In the guide, you will find our overall league table of UK universities as well as individual subject profiles and tables. We also have a special table showing you the universities and courses in England that recent graduates were least likely to regret.

The guide is packed with advice to help you make up your mind and start planning for university, from how to budget and which societies to join, to why more students are choosing to study psychology, and how to give your bedroom an Instagrammable glow-up. We also take a close look at why the University of Birmingham is rising up the league tables.

The rankings change annually, and some universities may benefit from temporary measures such as funding boosts or changes to their student intake. Don’t forget that universities languishing at the bottom of the overall table can be top for certain subjects – so check out our subject tables and profiles to build up a full picture. Remember that rankings are just one factor in your decision, among many others that are personal to you.
